April 16, 1917. 
Mr. Henry Fox may be reinstated as assistant engineer at $2,400 per annum in the Engineer Department at large, Little Rock, Ark., without regard to the length of time he has been separated from the service. Mr. Fox served about 14 years under the Engineer Department at large in various 
responsible positions and was furloughed on August 31, 1909. He has since been engaged in important engineer work in connection with rivers, harbors, and canals. In addition to his large experience in river and harbor work, he has passed several high-grade examinations for responsible positions in the classified service. His services are urgently required in connection with the completion of the survey of the Arkansas River, a difficult work and one which can not be satisfactorily performed except by a person having broad experience. nl Service Commission joins with the Secretary of War in recommending this order. 
April 18, 1917. 
Mr. D. Brockman Winfrey may be appointed a clerk in the competitive classified service of the Treasury Department without compliance with civil-service rules. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury, who states that Mr. Winfrey has been serving in the excepted position of private secretary to the Director of the Mint since November 11, 1915, and that on account of his thoroug knowledge of the general work of the Bureau of the Mint and the efficient manner 
in which he has performed his duties, it is believed that his permanent appointment will be in the interest of the service. 
May 7, 1917. 
Mrs. Annie Eopolucci may be appointed to a position as seamstress at the Wash- ington Navy Yard, without reference to the civil-service rules. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Navy, who states that Mrs. Eopolucci is the mother of John I. Eopolucci, formerly an enlisted man in the Navy, who was detailed as a gunner on the Aztec, and was the first person in the naval service of the United States to lose his life as the result of the sinking of an armed merchantman. 
May 7, 1917. : 
The appointment of Mr. Edgar Mabie as superintendent of the Bureau of War Risk Insurance in the Treasury Department is hereby authorized without compliance with civil-service rules. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury, who states that Mr. Mabie has had 14 years’ experience in one of the large insurance com- panies in New York City, passing on applications for insurance, examining policies, and having supervision of general office detail, and in view of the technical character of the work in the Bureau of War Risk Insurance, for which Jedially trained assistants are required, it is believed his appointment will be greatly in the interests of the service. 
May 8, 1917. 
‘William A. West may be appointed to the position of skilled laborer in the equip- ment shops, Post Office Department, without regard to civil-service rules and regu- lations.” ; The commission was not advised of the reasons for the issuance of the above order. 
May 9, 1917. 
Mr. Horace M. Albright may be appointed as Assistant Director of the National - Park Service. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Interior who states that Mr. Albright, as assistant attorney of the department, has been assisting in the management of the national park system for several years; that he is very familiar with the administration of the parks and with their problems; that he is personally acquainted with the field force and with the park concessioners who are 
under contract with the department to provide hotel accommodations and transporta-

The Civil Service Commission concurs in the recommendation for the issuance of this order. 
May 9, 1917. 
Henry S. Grogan, of Minnesota, may be reinstated as a post-office inspector without regard to the year limitation prescribed by Civil Service Rule IX. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Postmaster General because of Mr. Grogan’s long and efficient service in various branches of the Postal Service, including 11 years as a letter carrier and subsequent service from 1906 to 1912 as posto-flice inspector, superintendent of station, and assistant superintendent of mails. The Civil Service Commission concurs in the recommendation of the Postmaster General for an Executive order. 
June 12, 1917. 
Mrs. E. Anna Draper and Mrs. Katherine Gaines may be appointed as clerks in the Treasury Department for service in the Bureau of War Risk Insurance, without regard to civil-service requirements. EXCEPTION OF POSITIONS OF PRIVATE SECRETARIES OR CONFIDENTIAL CLERKS TO 
MEMBERS OF UNITED STATES RAILROAD LABOR BOARD. 
May 17, 1921. 
Schedule A of classified positions excepted from examination under Rule II, 
section 3, is hereby amended by the addition of the following: 
“ XVII. Railroad Labor Board: 
“1. One private secretary or confidential clerk to each member of the United 
States Railroad Labor Board.” 
. This order is issued upon recommendation of the United States Railroad 
Labor Board with the concurrence of the Civil Service Commission. 
EXCEPTION OF POSITION OF CLERK TO SIGN NAME OF SECRETARY OF INTERIOR TO 
TRIBAL DEEDS. 
July 29, 1921. ’ 
Schedule A, Subdivision VIII, of persons excepted from examination under

to be numbered 27, and to read as follows: 
“27. Clerk to sign under the direction of the Secretary, in his name and for 
him, his approval of all tribal deeds.” 
The Secretary of the Interior believes that the position should be within the 
excepted class because of the individual and confidential character of its duties. 
The Civil Service Commission concurs in recommending this order. 
EXCEPTION OF POSITIONS IN GUAM, SAMOA, AND VIRGIN ISLANDS. 
August 9, 1921. - 
Paragraph 7, Subdivision I, Schedule A, of the civil-service rules, is hereby 
amended by the insertion in line 1 of the words * or in the island of Guam, or 
in the island of Samoa, or in the Virgin Islands.” 
As amended the section will read: ; 
“ Any person employed in a foreign country, or in the island of Guam, or in 
the island of Samoa, or in the Virgin Islands, when in the opinion of the Civil 
Service Commission it is not practicable to treat the position as in the competi￾tive classified service; but this exception shall not apply to any person employed 
in a foreign country contiguous to the United States in the service of the Bureau 
of Immigration, Department of Labor.” 
Paragraph 3, Subdivision V, of Schedule A, will be stricken out as no longer 
necessary. This will have the effect of extending the exception of positions in 
these islands under the Navy Department to all the departments.

The first sentence of paragraph 2, Subdivision IV of Schedule A, of posi￾tions excepted from the requirement of examination under the civil service

who may be appointed without examination from $60 per month to $1,020 per 
annum. As amended, the paragraph will read as follows: 
“2. All telegraph operators and telegraph linemen receiving a monthly com￾pensation of $60 or less and cable seamen receiving not more than $1,020 per

ORDER RELATING TO THE RETIREMENT ACT OF MAY 22, 1920
EXCLUSION FROM THE OPERATION OF THE RETIREMENT ACT OF MAY 22, 1920, OF
SUBSTITUTES EMPLOYED TO HANDLE SEASONAL INCREASE IN MAIL AT SUMMER
AND WINTER RESORTS
March 22, 1926.
There are hereby excluded from the operation of the retirement act of May
22, 1920, because of their intermittent service, substitutes employed to handle
the seasonal increase in volume of mail at summer and winter resorts at such
post offices as may be specified by the Civil Service Commission with the
concurrence of the Post Office Department.
These substitutes shall be appointed in the same way as all others and shall
not receive promotion to a regular position without depositing in the retirement
fund the amount, with interest, which would have been deducted from their
compensation if they had not been treated as excluded under this order.

The Executive order of January 17, 1873, is hereby amended by the addition
of the following paragraph:
"In order that they may more efficiently function in the enforcement- of
the national prohibition act, any State, county, or municipal officer may be
appointed, at a nominal rate of compensation, as prohibition officer of the
Treasury Department to enforce the provisions of the national prohibition act
and acts supplemental thereto, in States and Territories except in those States
having constitutional or statutory provisions against State officers holding
office under the Federal Government."

REVOCATION OF THE EXECUTIVE ORDER OF MAY 21, 1921, AND CLASSIFICATION OF 
EMPLOYEES SERVING UNDER SUCH AUTHORIZATION 
December 8, 1928. 
Executive Order No. 3471, issued May 21, 1921, authorizing the Civil Service 
Commission to extend for single periods of a year or less the employments of 
qualified persons engaged on activities growing out of the World War which 
were temporary and diminishing in nature, is hereby revoked. 
Employees now in the service whose retention has been authorized under the 
order of May 21, 1921, are hereby covered into the classified service. 
This order is recommended by the War Department and concurred in by the 
Civil Service Commission. 
ORDER RELATING TO THE PROHIBITION SERVICE

EXAMINATION CLOSING NOVEMBER 20, 1928 
December 21, 1928. 
Until the ratings have been completed of the civil-service examination closing 
November 20, 1928, for positions of prohibition agent, the Secretary of the 
Treasury is hereby authorized, in his discretion, to continue under temporary 
appointment those prohibition agents, inspectors, and investigators entitled to 
military preference (1) whose applications for such examination have been 
accepted by the Civil Service Commission; and (2) who have been employed 
with clear records for at least two years in the prohibition service. 
For the purposes of this order, reinstatement may be made, in the discretion 
of the Secretary of the Treasury, of any preference employee herein described 
who was dropped from the prohbition service, without charges, subsequent to 
August 16, 1928.

The position of press helper in the Bureau of Engraving and Printing is 
hereby brought with the present incumbents into the competitive classified 
service. Vacancies in this position hereafter will be filled in accordance with 
the rules governing the classified civil service. 
This order is recommended by the Treasury Department and the Civil 
Service Commission.

(a) Unless otherwise provided hereinafter, an unclassified laborer may

in cases when in its opinion the circumstances are unusual, urgent, or in

NEWSPAPER READERS AND TRANSLATORS, 
October 25, 1917. 
Newspaper readers and translators selected by the Postmaster General for 
filling certain confidential positions under the trading-with-the-enemy act may 
be appointed during the period of the war with Germany without examination 
under the civil-service law. The Postmaster General states that there are 
available to the Post Office Department for appointment in these lines men 
whose loyalty has been proven and who in some cases will accept employment 
at a nominal salary through patriotic desire to give service at this time. 
The Civil Service Commission concurs in the issuance of this order in view 
of the highly confidential character of the employments and the particular 
qualifications required. 
FOOD AND FUEL ADMINISTRATIONS. 
November 10, 1917. 
In view of the fact that the Food Administration and the Fuel Administration 
are created to exist only during the present war with Germany, and that the 
temporary nature and the peculiarities of the work render it difficult and some￾times impossible to obtain from the competitive classified service of the United 
States eligibles for positions in these administrations, and because of conditions 
due to the war, such eligibles are often obtained only after delays which inter￾fere with work of an urgent nature, these administrations are authorized to 
employ for the period of the war without reference to the requirements of the 
civil-service laws and regulations such persons as in the judgment of those in 
responsible charge are best adapted to the work, it being understood that all possible use will be made of the Civil Service Commission and that this order 
shall not affect any person already employed by or certified to these administra￾tions under the civil-service laws and regulations.

the Civil Service Commission, one private secretary at $1,200 per annum to each 
State explosives inspector employed under the Administration of Explosives 
Inspection, act of Congress apprdved October 6, 1917, may be appointed without 
examination.

128 TWENTY-FIFTH REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION.
CLASSIFICATION OF VARIOUS PERSONS NOT HERETOFORE REPORTED AS CLASSIFIED.
October 9, 1908.
Prior to February 12, 1908, various places in the executive civil serivce were
filled without compliance with the requirements of the civil-service act and
rules, because the appointing officers were of the opinion that the terms of an
appropriation act or some circumstance implied exception from such require¬
ments. On February 12, 1908, the Attorney-General rendered an opinion hold¬
ing, in effect, that all places in the executive civil service, except those men¬
tioned in Schedule A of the rules, and except persons employed merely as
laborers, and persons whose appointments are subject to confirmation by the
Senate, must be filled as a result of open competitive examinations held under
the provisions of the law, and that Congress, in the exemption of any position
or class of positions from the operation of the civil-service act, must use lan¬
guage indicating clearly and affirmatively its intention that the civil-service
rules should not be applied.
Persons whose names are reported to the Civil Service Commission in response
to this opinion and who are occupying places whose duties are similar to those
of competitive positions may be classified upon approval by the commission, but
may be transferred only when, in the opinion of the Civil Service Commission,
such transfer is required in the interest of the service, and then only after an
appropriate examination by said commission. Vacancies shall be filled in
accordance with the civil-service act and rules. If said commission finds that
any of these places can not be satisfactorily subjected to competitive tests they
may be treated as excepted from examination and their occupants shall not
acquire a competitive status.
On February 12, 1908, the Attorney-General rendered an opinion which is
briefly described in the above order, and which the commission brought to the
attention of the heads of the several departments and offices, asking them to
report all positions which had not previously been reported as classified. Among
the most important classes of employees reported were those of the Commission
to the Five Civilized Tribes, consisting of clerks, stenographers, law clerks,
interpreters, watchmen, and messengers, in all 112 employees; persons connected
with logging operations of the General Land Office, consisting of superintendents
of logging, stenographers, bookkeepers, clerks, and timber scalers; employees
of national parks and reservations, consisting of scouts, rangers, animal keepers,
foresters, watchmen, supervisors, electricians, plumbers, gardeners, etc.; clerks
in the Bureau of Education paid from the general appropriation for education
in Alaska; additional farmers in the Indian Service; employees connected with
the allotting and irrigation projects in the Indian Service. In the Department
of State a law clerk and an assistant law clerk to audit the laws of Congress
were reported. In the Treasury Department a transportation clerk in the
office of the chief clerk and one plumber were reported. In the division of Reve¬
nue-Cutter Service two civilian instructors, one writer, three draftsmen, and
one superintendent of construction were reported. The instructors are employed
at Arundel Cove, Md., and the other persons in the office of the superintendent
of construction and repairs at Baltimore, Md. In the Department of Justice
an inspector and overseer in the United States penitentiary at Fort Leavenworth
were reported.
ORDERS AFFECTING UNCLASSIFIED LABORERS.
EXTENSION OF LABOR REGISTERS.
August 3, 1908.
Subdivision III, section 3, of the regulations to govern the employment of
unskilled laborers in federal offices outside of Washington, D. C., is hereby
amended by the addition of the following words: “ but eligible registers may
be extended for a longer time by direction of the Civil Service Commission,
when such action is deemed necessary in the interests of the service.”

TWENTY-FIFTH REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 129
The amended section will read as follows:
Sec. 3. The period of eligibility shall be one year from the date of entry
upon the register; but eligible registers may be extended for a longer time by
the direction of the Civil Service Commission, when such action is deemed
necessary in the interests of the service.
At various times the question of the advisability of extending labor registers
for a longer period than one year had been given consideration by the com¬
mission. The conclusion was finally reached that the exigencies of the service,
the infrequency of appointments, and the pressure of work on the district secre¬
taries are such at times as to render it desirable and advisable that the com¬
mission should have discretionary power to extend a register for a period
beyond one year. In cases where such extensions are authorized the post￾office addresses of the eligibles will be verified anew and the parties certified
for appointment can be required to appear for a new physical examination to
insure their being in proper physical condition to perform the duties of the
position to which they are appointed.
LABORERS OUTSIDE OF WASHINGTON, D. C.
October 21, 1908.
The regulations governing the employment of unskilled laborers in federal
offices outside of Washington, D. C., are hereby amended, viz:
1. By adding a new regulation, to be numbered VI, and to read as follows:
VI.—Demotions, Transfers, and Extensions of Temporary Service.
Section 1. The Civil Service Commission shall have authority to authorize:
(a) The demotion of any person from the classified service to the position
of mere unskilled laborer, and the appointment of such person, in consequence
of such demotion, upon his passing the required physical examination, to the
position of mere unskilled laborer; a statement of duties in every case to be
attached to the application of the department for such demotion, showing the
duties of the person proposed to be demoted in the old and new position.
(ft) The transfer of any mere unskilled laborer from any office or bureau
to another, provided that such unskilled laborer is in good standing and has
had at least six months’ experience, and the qualifications in the new position
are the same as those in the old.
(c) The temporary appointment of a mere unskilled laborer for a period to
exceed thirty days in cases of great and evident necessity.

~The commission does not find the status of such person clearly defined by 
‘statute or by the civil service rules established by the President under the 
powers conferred upon him by statute. 
Section 7 of the act of March 15, 1898 (30 Stat., 316) provides for leave 
with pay,’ in the discretion of the head of a department, for not more than 
thirty days in one calendar year to any or all employees. A proviso of the 
same section vests in the head of a department the further discretionary power 
to grant an employee, under certain conditions, an additional leave of absence 
with pay for a second period of not more than thirty days in any calendar year. 
It is to be noted that the periods above provided for are both “leaves with 
pay.” No leave without pay is expressly provided for or defined. The only 
reference to such a status is the negative provision that an employee borne on 
the rolls of the department after the expiration of such leave with pay shall 
. not be entitled to pay ‘ during the period of such excessive absence.” 
The case of an employee who desires to be absent from actual service and 
who is not cared for by the statute above referred to providing for leave with 
pay is expressly provided for under Rule IX of the President’s rules governing 
the classified civil service, under which such employee, assuming separation 
from the service without delinquency or misconduct, may be reinstated by the 
department within one year from the date of such separation. This gives to 
the employee a status for reinstatement and to the department the discretionary 
power to reinstate, the initiative resting solely with the department. Both 
status and right are limited to one year from date of separation, actual rein- statement requiring a precedent ascertainment and certification by the Civil 
Service Commission that the employee is eligible for reinstatement under the 
rule. 
Cases arose in which the employee did not desire to accept a status in which 
restoration to the service was to be dependent on the affirmative exercise of a 
purely discretionary power at a future time by the then head of the depart￾ment, and in which the head of the department was willing at the time of the 
contemplated separation to exercise his discretionary power in the present 
to become effective at a fixed time in the future. This was contrived as a means of creating a distinct status of nonservice and nonpay to be terminated 
within the time limit by the mere return of the employee to actual service. 
So long as leave without service or pay was limited to one year from date of 
separation from service, it constituted an anticipatory exercise of a right that 
would in every case be approved by the Civil Service Commission and was 
deemed to be no substantial variance from the rule. The departments desired 
in many cases to give to employees about to leave the service the sense of 
security that was carried by “leave without pay ” as distinguished from formal 
separation from the service and formal reinstatement on the initiative of the 
department at a future time. 
The practice was resorted to from time to time in the several departments. 
By common consent it was limited to a maximum period of one year sO as 
to respect the limitation in the reinstatement rule. By like common consent 
in case the employee failed to return to a status of actual service within a

regarded as absolute. It was the universal practice, after the expiration of one 
year without return to actual service, and upon a desire by the department to make a formal reinstatement, to send the case to the Civil Service Commis￾sion to ascertain and certify the employee's status for reinstatement. This 
practice did in a sense respect the reinstatement rule, while in practical effect 
it enabled a department to give to an employee a full year of absence in addi￾tion to the year provided for by Rule IX. It doubled the period of absence 
and reinstatement by departmental practice and common consent. This was 
deemed to be the utmost limit of liberality possible under the law. 
On July 28, 1916, the Congress enacted a statute in relation to employees of 
the Post Office Department, which is a legislative recognition of the depart￾mental practice of “leave without pay.” Since it carries the same limit of 
one year from separation, this act merely gave express direction for the main￾tenance in one department of a practice long continued in all departments, 
and did not modify the attitude or practice of the Civil Service Commission 
in any case. 
In so far as the rights of employees absent on ‘leave without pay” rest on 
a departmental practice, they are confined within the limitations of the prac￾tice, which make the separation absolute at the end of one year. Rights of 
postal employees created by the act above referred to are expressly limited to the 
period of one year. Before and at the time when the retirement act was 
passed the most liberal possible view of the status of employees on “leave 
without pay ” under existing law and practice was: 
(1) That an employee separated from actual service on “leave without pay ” 
was constructively in the civil service, to wit: In a status of nonservice and non￾pay to be terminated by return to actual service within the year, or to become 
absolute by failure to return to actual service within the year.

TWENTY-SIXTH REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 129 
Mr. Longan was appointed as a clerk at $1,000 per annum for duty as confidential clerk 
in the office of the Postmaster-General on July 10, 1907, under an exception from exam￾ination contained in Schedule A of the civil-service rules. The Postmaster-General 
stated that Mr. Longan had developed exceptional qualifications which made it very 
desirable to retain him as a permanent employee in the classified service, and that he 
was also an efficient stenographer and typewriter, in which capacity he had rendered 
very faithful service. 
March 2, 1909. 
Mr. James Mullenbach may be appointed inspector in charge of information and distribution work, Immigration Service, Chicago, Ill., without examination under the civil-service rules, in view of his peculiar qualifications for the work involved. 
Mr. Mullenbach was very highly recommended to the Department of Commerce 
and Labor as the most thoroughly equipped man that could be found for the position 
in question. For four years preceding his appointment he had been the superin￾tendent of the Municipal Lodging House at Chicago, and prior to that time was for 
two years a resident of Chicago Commons, a social settlement located in one of the con￾gested foreign districts of Chicago. He was thoroughly acquainted with conditions 
in Chicago, had traveled abroad considerably, and through his experience in dealing 
with the immigrant lodger was equipped to render the best possible service in the posi￾tion to which he was appointed. The Secretary of Commerce and Labor urgently 
recommended Mr. Mullenbach’s appointment through executive order. 
Under date of March 30, 1909, Mr. Mullenbach declined the appointment. 
March 24, 1909. 
Mr. F. B. Simons may be reinstated as a clerk in the Bureau of Internal Revenue without reference to the length of time since his separation from the service. This order is made to enable the Commissioner of Internal Revenue to secure a civil servant + with the needed technical knowledge for cases involving denatured alcohol. It is made upon the recommendation of the Civil Service Commission, the Secretary of the Treasury, and the Commissioner of Internal Revenue. 
Mr. F. B. Simons was appointed a clerk in the Bureau of Internal Revenue in 1900 
and resigned in 1906, and was therefore ineligible for reinstatement, as his year of 
eligibility had expired. The Commissioner of Internal Revenue in recommending 
the order stated that although rated as a clerk, Mr. Simons had been assigned as 
assistant in the chemical division on account of his training as a chemist, and that 
his work there was of the highest order, involving the charge and conduct of the 
laboratory in the absence of the chemist in charge, the taxing of oleomargarine and 
renovated butter, and other measures requiring chemical work. Because of his 
experience Mr. Simons would be very valuable in the laboratory of the bureau and 
as an expert witness in connection with the work incident to making analyses of 
oleomargarine and distilled spirits where controversies arise on these subjects and are 
pending in court. 
May 25, 1909. 
Mr. F. B. Simons may be reinstated in the service of the Treasury Department as an analytical chemist in the office of the appraiser of merchandise at Baltimore, Md., without regard to the length of time since his separation from the service. This order 
is made to enable the Secretary of the Treasury to secure a civil servant for a vacant place in the office above named, who is peculiarly well fitted for the performance of its duties by reason of his ten years’ service as a chemist in the Division of Chemistry 
in the Bureau of Internal Revenue. The executive order of March 24, 1909 (No. 1053), authorizing the reinstatement of Mr. irons in the Bureau of Internal Revenue, Treasury Department, is hereby 
revoked. 
April 6, 1909.

the office of the Secretary of the United States Senate from June 30, 1905, to March 31, 1909, may be reinstated in an appropriate position in the classified service. 
Mr Garver was appointed on July 3, 1904, as a forest assistant in the General Land 
Office. He was transferred by act of Congress, with his position, to the Department of 
Agriculture on February 1, 1905, from which department he resigned on June 26, 1905. 
From that date until March 31, 1909, he served as a clerk in the office of the Secretary 
of the United States Senate. Civil-service Rule X, paragraph 3, provides that any 
person may be retransferred to a position in which he was formerly employed or to any 
position to which transfer could be made therefrom if, since his transfer, he has been 
continuously in the executive or judicial civil service of the United States or of its 
insular possessions. As Mr. Garver had been serving in the legislative service the 
provisions of this rule did not permit his retransfer, but there appeared to be no reason 
why he should not logically be entitled to retransfer, and the Commission recom￾mended the issuance of the above order. 
April 7, 1909. 
Mrs. Nannie M. Wayland may be reinstated in the classified service in the Treasury Department without regard to the length of time that she has been separated from the service. 
Mrs. Wayland had formerly served as a clerk in the Treasury Department, but was 
separated by resignation on April 19, 1907. On November 27 of that year the Com￾mission authorized her reinstatement in the Treasury Department, with a view to 
her immediate transfer to the Philippine service. Mrs. Wayland was not transferred 
to the Philippine service under this authority, but did serve for a short period in the 
federal service in the Philippines. Her year of eligibility for reinstatement expired 
on April 19, 1908, and the above executive order was necessary to authorize her rein￾statement after that date. 
April 16, 1909. 
Mr. Archibald S. Pinkett, of Pennsylvania, may be appointed to a clerkship in the Department of State without examination under the civil-service act and rules. This order is made at the request and upon the recommendation of the Secretary of State, who has knowledge of Mr. Pinkett’s fitness from his clerical service under the Secretary while he was a Senator in Congress.
